extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, students, and general readers interested in humor
extracted.subtask_description: A reference list and brief explanations of techniques and structures (devices) used to make something funny, with examples and notes on how each device creates humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic device (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedic device is a technique or structure used to make something funny. They are often used in comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as the umbrella concept for all listed devices; indicates that devices are techniques/structures rather than single joke forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition is the essential comedic device and is often used in combination with other devices to reinforce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the 'callback'—recalling a statement or theme as the punchline or close of a scene; 'Englishman, Irishman, and Scotsman' jokes where repetition sets up a modus operandi and builds tension before a resolving juxtaposition. Repetition creates tension and release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole (overstatement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperbole, an overstatement, is a figure of speech in which statements are exaggerated or extravagant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be used to reflect or effect strong feelings or impressions; functions by amplifying reality to comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understatement
rubrics_metrics.description: An understatement is a figure of speech in which statements are purposely understated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May indicate the speaker's nonchalance or obliviousness regarding an important or remarkable situation; often results in irony when the speaker's response does not match audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double entendre
rubrics_metrics.description: A double entendre is a spoken phrase that can be understood in either of two ways: an innocent literal meaning and a figurative meaning that is often ironic or risqué.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relies on the audience having additional knowledge to understand the secondary meaning; commonly used for risqué or ironic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun
rubrics_metrics.description: A pun consists of a deliberate confusion of similar words or phrases for humorous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can rely on homonymy (equivalence of similar words), polysemy (different shades of meaning of one word), or a clash of literal meaning with a metaphor; used to create wordplay-based humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtaposition is a literary technique which causes the audience to compare two elements simply because they are placed next to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the comparison is unexpected it creates irony; can be produced through grammatical ambiguity. (See incongruous juxtaposition theory.) Example concept: success and failure placed together to create an unexpected comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaken identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistaken identity (often of one twin for another) is a centuries-old comedic device used by Shakespeare and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mistake can be an intended deception or an accident. Modern examples: The Parent Trap, The Truth About Cats and Dogs, Sister, Sister, Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen films; other examples include The Government Inspector and adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taboo
rubrics_metrics.description: Taboo involves saying something that nobody else would say in a civilized environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being disgusting or politically wrong in front of an audience can surprise and shock (e.g., jokes about pedophiles); there is a liberating element to breaking social norms, but it relies on shock and boundary-crossing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic timing is the use of pacing and delivery to enhance the effectiveness of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include inserting a dramatic pause or beat to let the audience discern subtext, and creating laughs from quick juxtaposition between fast and slow timing. Example: George Carlin's delivery in 'Seven Words You Can't Say On Television.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick
rubrics_metrics.description: Slapstick is a type of comedy involving exaggerated physical violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically used by performers like Buster Keaton, Charlie Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy, the Keystone Cops, the Three Stooges; common in animated cartoons such as Tom and Jerry and Looney Tunes. Functions via exaggerated physical action and visual gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdirection
rubrics_metrics.description: Misdirection is when a comedian leads the audience to expect one thing and then pulls the rug out from under them during the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often combined with other devices (taboo, mistaken identity). Example cited: a controversial 2011 Jimmy Carr tweet that combined taboo, mistaken identity, and misdirection. Relies on setting up an expectation and violating it for surprise.
